sources_new_this_agent.source_name: BS 7671:2018+A2:2022 — Requirements for Electrical Installations (IET Wiring Regulations 18th Edition, Amendment 2)
sources_new_this_agent.organisation: British Standards Institution (BSI) / Institution of Engineering and Technology (IET)
sources_new_this_agent.publication_date: 2022-03 (in force since 28 March 2023 for all new work)
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Statutory reference standard cited by Approved Document P. Amendment 2 introduced RCD protection extended to lighting circuits in dwellings, AFDD requirements (with lighting-circuit omission where unexpected disconnection could cause danger), SPD default installation. Reg 522.6 governs cables in walls/partitions (50mm depth rule).

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: Approved Document P — Electrical safety, dwellings (2013 edition, England)
sources_new_this_agent.organisation: MHCLG / Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Statutory guidance. Notifiable work in dwellings limited to new circuits from consumer unit and additions in special locations. Alteration/extension of existing lighting circuits generally non-notifiable but must still comply with BS 7671.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: CIBSE / SLL Lighting Guide 16 — Lighting for stairs (2017)
sources_new_this_agent.organisation: Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers (CIBSE) — Society of Light and Lighting (SLL)
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Primary UK design guide for stair lighting. Aligns with BS EN 12464-1 values. Referenced by architects, M&E consultants and lighting designers.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: SLL Code for Lighting (2022 edition)
sources_new_this_agent.organisation: CIBSE / Society of Light and Lighting
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Umbrella UK lighting code. Contains stair illuminance recommendations differentiated by building type; values derive from BS EN 12464-1.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: BS EN 12464-1:2021 — Light and lighting. Lighting of work places. Indoor work places
sources_new_this_agent.notes: European standard cited in CIBSE guidance. Contains published lux values for indoor stairs (commonly reported as 100–150 lux depending on task/context). Used where a published lux figure must be quoted.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: BS 5266-1:2016 — Emergency lighting. Code of practice for the emergency escape lighting of premises
sources_new_this_agent.publication_date: 2016 (with 2024-updated companion standards BS EN 50172:2024 and BS EN 1838:2024)
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Governs emergency escape lighting to and from escape stairs. Does NOT cover single private dwellings but applies to common access routes in multi-storey dwellings, HMOs and non-domestic premises.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: BS EN 60529 — Degrees of protection provided by enclosures (IP Code)
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Defines the two-digit IP rating system used to specify moisture/dust ingress protection for stair light fittings and drivers. IP20 typical indoor · IP44 splash · IP65 jets · IP67 immersion.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: BS EN 60669-2-1 — Switches for household and similar fixed electrical installations. Particular requirements. Electronic switches
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Product standard applied to PIR motion sensor switches and electronic time-delay controllers used in stair-lighting automation. Compliance frequently declared alongside BS EN 55015 (EMC / radio disturbance).

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: BS EN IEC 62386 — Digital Addressable Lighting Interface (DALI)
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Category-level reference for addressable/dimmable stair-light control (relevant to commercial/spec-heavy installs). Consumer smart systems (Zigbee, Matter, Thread, Z-Wave, Wi-Fi) sit alongside DALI in the wider ecosystem.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: IES LM-80 & IES TM-21 — LED lumen maintenance test and projection methods
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Industry method for measuring LED lumen depreciation (LM-80) and extrapolating rated life at L70/L80/L90 (TM-21). Underpins the 25,000/50,000/70,000-hour ratings quoted on stair-light datasheets.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: Collingwood Lighting — Step Lights product category (UK manufacturer datasheets)
sources_new_this_agent.notes: UK manufacturer datasheet category — publishes step-light IP ratings, lamp-life hours (up to 70,000h stated), warranty terms (up to 7 years). Category-level source per governance rule; not endorsing a single product.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: JCC Lighting — domestic and commercial LED fittings (UK manufacturer datasheets)
sources_new_this_agent.notes: UK manufacturer widely specified by electricians. Datasheet category source for stair/step/downlight fittings. Category-level reference only.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: MEAN WELL — LED driver product families (HLG, ELG, LPV, APV series)
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Industry-dominant LED driver datasheets covering CV, CC, CV+CC drivers in 12V/24V/36V/48V/54V with IP20 through IP67 options. Category-level reference for constant-voltage vs constant-current driver selection.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: Philips Signify — Philips Hue smart lighting technical support (Zigbee + Matter bridge)
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Category-level reference for consumer smart lighting on Zigbee protocol with Matter bridge. Widely used for retrofit smart control of stair fittings via existing Hue Bridge.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: NICEIC — Approved Contractor / Domestic Installer scheme (Certsure LLP)
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Government-approved Part P competent-person scheme for self-certification of notifiable electrical work in dwellings. Also publishes technical newsletters on BS 5266 and other stair-relevant topics.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: NAPIT — Competent Person Scheme (NAPIT Certification Ltd)
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Government-approved Part P competent-person scheme alongside NICEIC. Same statutory authority to self-certify notifiable domestic electrical work.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: BS 6387 — Test method for resistance to fire of cables required to maintain circuit integrity under fire conditions
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Fire-resistant cable test standard (CWZ highest classification). Relevant where stair lighting forms part of a protected escape route requiring circuit integrity during fire — typically non-domestic and common areas of flats.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: BS EN 60332-3 & BS EN 61034-2 — Reduced fire propagation and low smoke emission from cables
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Cited by BS 7671 Reg 422.2.1 — cables on escape routes must satisfy these standards for reduced fire propagation and low smoke emission. Underpins LSZH cable specification for stair enclosures in common areas.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: Historic England — Building Regulations and Historic Buildings guidance (electrical services in listed buildings)
sources_new_this_agent.notes: Reference for retrofitting stair lighting to listed / heritage stairs where cable routing and fabric alteration require conservation consent.

sources_new_this_agent.source_name: HSE — HSG38 Lighting at Work
sources_new_this_agent.notes: HSE workplace lighting guidance covering minimum/average illuminance for workplace areas including stairs. Companion to HSE L24 ACOP.

Design accent — architectural lighting as a design feature
Wayfinding / navigation in low-ambient conditions

summary_topics_evidenced: Reduced trip/fall risk on stairs (safety benefit — HSE / BS 5266 rationale)
Task illumination targeted at tread nosings (CIBSE LG16 intent)
Energy efficiency of LED vs incandescent/halogen (LED at ~7–10W to match 50W halogen output)
Long service life reducing re-lamping frequency (LM-80/TM-21 rated hours)
Design feature and property value perception (trade press only — not primary evidenced)

Requires access panel / driver location planning for future serviceability

Flicker/dimming compatibility issues with mains dimmers
Retrofit disruption to plaster / decoration / stair fabric
Failure of driver typically ends product life for sealed fittings

summary_topics_evidenced: LED replacements for halogen equivalents consume approximately 80–90% less energy for equivalent lumen output (trade/industry sources synthesising manufacturer datasheets)
Typical LED stair-step light draws single-digit watts (fitting datasheets category — MEAN WELL driver + Collingwood / JCC fittings)
kWh consumption depends on fitting count · dwell/duty cycle · sensor/timer control regime — no single canonical figure applies

source_coverage.wattage_efficacy_comparison: Strong — long-established manufacturer/industry consensus, cross-cited by BSI, LIA, Energy Saving Trust equivalents.
source_coverage.specific_home_kWh_prescription: NOT provided — governance rule: no prescriptive energy figures without a directly quotable published source per installation.

summary_topics_evidenced: LED lamps commonly rated 25,000 to 50,000 hours (industry standard range per LM-80/TM-21 method)
Premium UK step-light manufacturers publish up to 70,000 hours (Collingwood category datasheets, backed by warranties up to 7 years)
L70 = 70% initial lumen output remaining · L80 = 80% remaining · L90 = 90% remaining · industry end-of-life threshold typically L70
Rated lifespan applies to the LED chip — the driver commonly fails first and is often the actual life-limiter for a fitting

source_coverage.manufacturer_rated_hours: Strong (Collingwood, JCC, MEAN WELL datasheet categories)
source_coverage.real_world_field_data: Not obtained in this pass — no independent UK long-term field study located

summary_topics_evidenced: Constant-voltage (CV) drivers (12V/24V DC) used for LED strip and multiple step-light fittings on a shared bus
Constant-current (CC) drivers used for individual downlight-style fittings rated in mA
CV+CC combined-mode drivers common in outdoor IP67 series
LED chip binning (colour temperature and output) drives uniformity — bin-matched fittings avoid visible tread-to-tread variance

source_coverage.driver_selection: Strong (MEAN WELL, Downlights Direct, general electrician trade press)
source_coverage.chip_binning_uniformity: Moderate — component-manufacturer level, less commonly surfaced in end-user guidance

summary_topics_evidenced: Zigbee (Philips Hue), Z-Wave, Thread, Matter and Wi-Fi are the principal consumer smart-lighting protocols
Matter is the cross-vendor interoperability layer coming into widespread deployment through 2025–2026
DALI (BS EN IEC 62386) is the commercial/spec addressable protocol

source_coverage.protocol_landscape: Strong (Matter Alpha, Zigbee Alliance, Philips Hue manufacturer docs)
source_coverage.stair_specific_smart_integration: Weak — no independent standards body publishes a stair-specific smart-lighting integration guide

summary_topics_evidenced: PIR sensor switches for stair lighting are governed by product standard BS EN 60669-2-1 (electronic switches) plus BS EN 55015 for EMC/radio disturbance
Dedicated stair-lighting PIR controllers commonly offer 1–30 minute time-delays and 2-way switch compatibility
Multi-channel stair controllers (e.g. 16/32-step) exist that sequence tread illumination on detection

source_coverage.wiring_installation_procedure: OUT OF SCOPE per governance rule — will not be reproduced

summary_topics_evidenced: Time-clock control, IR/RF remote, and smartphone/app control are common consumer options
Consumer smart bridges (Hue, LIFX) enable schedule-based automation
DALI addressable control provides scheduling in commercial installations
Matter bridging (via Hue Bridge, SmartThings, Home Assistant, Alexa/Google) unifies previously siloed lighting ecosystems
Voice control via Alexa, Google Assistant, Apple Home is standard on major consumer smart-lighting SKUs

source_coverage.vendor_documentation: Strong (Signify, Amazon, Google, Apple public support pages)

summary_topics_evidenced: Colour temperature is measured in Kelvin (K) — lower K = warmer / more amber, higher K = cooler / more blue
Warm white 2700K–3000K is the dominant residential recommendation for staircase interior lighting (lighting-industry trade press consensus)
4000K neutral and 5000K+ cool white are more common in commercial escape stairs and industrial contexts
CRI (Colour Rendering Index) ≥80 typical for domestic; ≥90 preferred for material-appearance-critical settings

source_coverage.kelvin_definition_and_bands: Strong (BS EN 12464-1, CIBSE SLL Code, manufacturer datasheets)
source_coverage.specific_residential_K_recommendation: Trade press consensus — no single UK standard prescribes a specific K value for domestic stairs

summary_topics_evidenced: BS EN 12464-1 publishes maintained illuminance values for indoor stairs (widely reported at 100 lux minimum in older editions and 150 lux in more recent guidance, differentiated by task and building type)
CIBSE SLL Code for Lighting and LG16 differentiate stair lux by building type (residential, commercial, industrial)
BS 5266-1 requires minimum 1 lux average along escape route floor with higher levels at stairs, changes in direction, exits and firefighting equipment locations

source_coverage.published_lux_values: Strong — governance rule permits quoting these figures because they come from named published standards

summary_topics_evidenced: BS 5266-1:2016 (with BS EN 50172:2024 and BS EN 1838:2024) is the UK code of practice for emergency escape lighting of premises
Applies to escape stairs in non-domestic premises, HMOs, and COMMON areas of multi-storey dwellings — does NOT cover the interior of a single private dwelling
Approved Document B (Fire Safety) references emergency escape lighting for buildings other than dwellings and for common areas of flats
Fire-resistant cable standards BS 6387 (CWZ classification) and low-smoke standards BS EN 60332-3 / BS EN 61034-2 apply where lighting circuits serve protected escape routes

source_coverage.escape_lighting_code_of_practice: Strong (BS 5266-1 verified via websearch, NICEIC published summary)

_section_meta.scope: Best stage during manufacture · best stage during installation · retrofit · running cables · concealing cables · LED drivers · transformers · access panels · serviceability · moisture protection (IP) · fire · BS 7671 · Part P · common installation mistakes.
_section_meta.content_style_reminder: NEX brain must NOT reproduce wiring procedure. All install steps → expert_experience_required or route to a Part P registered electrician.

summary_topics_evidenced: Trade convention: cable chases / conduit runs and mortices for fittings are routed into strings, risers and newels at the joinery bench BEFORE assembly and finishing — this is not documented in any single BSI/BS standard but is universal shop-floor practice reflected across UK stair-manufacturer marketing and installer forums.
Pre-wiring at manufacture allows factory-tested fittings and hidden cable termination points to be prepared for site electrician to connect

source_coverage.published_standard: None located — this is craft workflow knowledge, not standardised process

summary_topics_evidenced: Sequence with first-fix electrical: cable back-boxes, driver locations and control-cable routes must be co-ordinated with joiner before staircase is fixed, otherwise access is lost after balustrade and skirting are fitted
Second-fix (lighting fitting installation and commissioning) happens after decoration

source_coverage.published_standard: None — trade sequencing knowledge, referenced generically in electrician trade press but not codified

summary_topics_evidenced: Retrofit requires lifting floorboards or cutting chases through plaster; BS 7671 522.6 safe-zone rules apply to cables buried <50mm from wall/partition surface (RCD 30mA protection required if outside prescribed zones or <50mm depth)
For listed / heritage stairs, cable routing may require conservation consent (Historic England technical advice)

source_coverage.heritage_constraints: Strong (Historic England, referenced via src-018 in source_catalogue)

summary_topics_evidenced: BS 7671 prescribes safe zones for concealed cables in walls and partitions — vertical/horizontal from accessories, 150mm strips at wall/ceiling and wall/wall corners
Cables <50mm depth outside a safe zone must be mechanically protected (earthed metallic sheath, capping) or protected by 30mA RCD
Cables run under floorboards should be clipped to joists at ~50mm below top of joist to avoid nail damage; drilling joists is generally preferred to notching to preserve structural integrity

source_coverage.practical_routing_technique: Moderate — DIY / trade guidance is consistent but detailed procedure is out-of-scope per governance rule (no wiring instructions in brain content)

summary_topics_evidenced: Modern LED installations use electronic LED drivers, not iron-core transformers
Constant-voltage drivers (12V/24V DC) power LED strip and multi-fitting DC buses; constant-current drivers (rated in mA) power individual downlight-style fittings
Drivers must be sized with headroom (industry convention ~20% additional capacity) — sustained loading at 100% shortens driver life
Drivers should be installed in accessible, ventilated locations — sealed voids and under-tread cavities without airflow can cause premature failure

source_coverage.driver_topology_and_sizing: Strong (MEAN WELL, Downlights Direct, general LED driver technical literature)

summary_topics_evidenced: BS 7671 requires that terminations, joints and control gear remain accessible for inspection, testing and maintenance unless installed in an approved maintenance-free enclosure
Manufacturer application notes consistently warn against sealing drivers into inaccessible cavities — driver failure is the most common life-limiting event
IP rating format defined by BS EN 60529: first digit = solids/dust ingress, second digit = liquid ingress
IP20 typical for dry indoor step lights (no dust protection at particle level, no moisture protection)
IP44 minimum for many bathroom Zone-2 and near-splash applications
IP65 for direct water-jet exposure (wet zones, outdoor covered locations)
IP67 for temporary immersion (external hardscape, buried driver enclosures)
Where stair lighting adjoins bathroom Zone 1 or 2, bathroom IP zoning rules per BS 7671 Section 701 apply

source_coverage.zoning_application: Strong (BS 7671 Section 701 for bathrooms; manufacturer datasheet categories for stair/step fittings)

summary_topics_evidenced: Approved Document B Volume 1 (dwellings) and Volume 2 (non-dwellings) govern fire safety of escape routes including stairs
BS 7671 Reg 422.2.1: cables on escape routes must satisfy BS EN 60332-3 (reduced flame propagation) and BS EN 61034-2 (low smoke emission)
BS 6387 (CWZ classification) applies to cables required to maintain circuit integrity during a fire — typically emergency escape lighting and fire-fighting supplies
Fire-rated downlights are commonly required where fittings penetrate a fire-resistant ceiling below a protected stair

source_coverage.regulatory: Strong (Approved Document B src-002, BS 7671 Reg 422)

summary_topics_evidenced: All fixed electrical installations in England and Wales dwellings must comply with BS 7671 (current: 18th Edition + Amendment 2)
Approved Document P (England) applies to dwellings; notifiable work now limited to new circuits from consumer unit + additions in special locations (bathrooms, outdoors)
Alterations/extensions to existing lighting circuits are typically non-notifiable but still require BS 7671 compliance and an Electrical Installation Certificate or Minor Works Certificate

Registered installer with a Government-approved Competent Person Scheme (NICEIC, NAPIT, BESCA, Blue Flame, Certsure, OFTEC) can self-certify notifiable work; otherwise notification to Building Control is required before starting
Undersized driver — causes flicker, dim output, premature failure
Sealed / unventilated driver location — thermal stress shortens life
Driver not accessible after finishing — non-compliant with BS 7671 accessibility requirement
Incompatible dimmer paired with LED driver — flicker, buzz, driver damage
Wrong IP rating for location (indoor-rated fitting in bathroom Zone 1/2 or external staircase)
Cables run outside safe zones or <50mm without RCD protection or mechanical protection
Colour temperature or bin mismatch producing visibly uneven step-to-step illumination

source_coverage.driver_and_flicker: Strong (LEDVANCE, MEAN WELL, general industry consensus)
source_coverage.aesthetic_bin_mismatch: Moderate — well-known to specifiers but not formally documented in end-user guidance

_section_meta.scope: LED replacement · driver replacement · lifespan · cleaning · troubleshooting · water damage · power failures · future proofing · availability of replacement fittings.
_section_meta.content_style_reminder: NEX brain must direct users to a Part P registered electrician for any mains-side maintenance. No wiring procedure will be authored.

summary_topics_evidenced: Sealed LED fittings (integrated LED, no user-replaceable lamp) are the dominant modern product form — end-of-life means fitting replacement, not lamp swap
Retrofit LED lamps (GU10, MR16, E27, B22) can be user-changed in socketed fittings

source_coverage.manufacturer_datasheet_category: Strong (Collingwood, JCC and similar UK manufacturers)

summary_topics_evidenced: Driver failure is the most common life-limiting event — often before the LED itself has reached L70
Replacement drivers must match voltage/current/wattage of original and are the province of a competent electrician
Remote drivers (not integral to fitting) are more serviceable than integrated / sealed drivers

source_coverage.replacement_procedure: OUT OF SCOPE per governance rule

summary_topics_evidenced: LED chip: 25,000 to 70,000+ hours depending on drive current and thermal management (LM-80/TM-21 method)
LED driver: highly variable, commonly the earliest failure point; lifetime strongly influenced by operating temperature and load factor
Warranty typically 2–7 years on UK residential stair-light fittings (varies by manufacturer/product tier)
Dust/fingerprints on lenses/covers reduce measurable output — routine dry-cloth cleaning is a standard maintenance step
Wet cleaning must observe the fitting's IP rating (IP20 fittings must not be sprayed)

source_coverage.no_formal_published_stair_light_cleaning: None located — general LIA / manufacturer good-practice guidance only

summary_topics_evidenced: Common symptoms and probable causes (flicker, cold-start dim, buzzing, intermittent operation) are well documented at manufacturer/industry level
First check: loose connection or terminal contact (industry consensus)
Persistent problems with heat, burning smell, breaker trips → isolate the circuit and call a qualified electrician (industry safety consensus)

source_coverage.manufacturer_troubleshooting_notes: Strong (LEDVANCE, MEAN WELL, other industry sources)

summary_topics_evidenced: Water ingress beyond the fitting's IP rating causes corrosion of solder joints, electrolytic corrosion of driver components, and short-circuit risk
Fitting must be de-energised before inspection following water ingress
Replacement rather than repair is the norm for water-damaged sealed LED fittings

source_coverage.ingress_mechanism: Well-established (BS EN 60529 IP classification, industry consensus)

summary_topics_evidenced: In domestic dwellings there is no statutory backup requirement for interior stair lighting
In non-domestic premises and common escape routes of HMOs / blocks of flats, BS 5266-1 emergency escape lighting must remain operational for a minimum specified duration (published in the standard)
Battery-backup luminaires and central-battery systems are the two principal emergency-lighting topologies
Remote (non-integral) drivers, standard fitting cut-out sizes and standard DC voltages (12V/24V) improve future replaceability
Matter-compliant smart controls reduce vendor lock-in risk for stair-lighting automation over long service life
Documenting driver model / fitting model / colour temperature / bin (where known) at handover assists like-for-like replacement years later

source_coverage.documentation_at_handover: Craft convention — no formal standard mandates this for domestic stair lighting

summary_topics_evidenced: Product-line churn is high in the LED sector — a specific stair fitting SKU may be discontinued within 3–7 years

Choosing established UK manufacturers (Collingwood, JCC, Aurora, Ansell, Knightsbridge, LEDVANCE, Signify) with long-lived platforms reduces obsolescence risk (industry observation, not a certified guarantee)
Warranty periods (2–7 years) do not equal replacement-availability periods — the two are distinct

source_coverage.no_formal_published_data_on_SKU_lifecycl: None located — observation is industry-consensus rather than standard
